source_first_audit.profile_reason: Common polysemous noun/verb with bounded logic, property/legal, story, pronunciation, and etymology extensions.

coverage_axes.notes: Independent general and specialist dictionaries cover the six article sense families, including work-premise and property-premises uses.
Sources cover noun/verb behavior, premise A on B, proposition-as-premise use, clause-taking use, and verb inflections.
The British spelling variant and the directly relevant inflected/plural forms are independently attested.
Logic and legal/property uses are explicitly covered by general and legal references.

Formal labeling, British spelling qualification, and UK/US pronunciation information provide the relevant register/region evidence; numeric learner frequency scores remain editorial estimates for later review.
Pronunciation variants, plural pronunciation, Latin origin, and the historical property-sense pathway are covered.

facts.statement: in logic, a proposition serves as a basis of argument or inference, including a syllogistic premise
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster defines the logic sense as a proposition supposed or proved prior as a basis of argument or inference.

facts.statement: a premise can be something assumed or taken for granted
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster separately records the broader assumed-or-taken-for-granted sense.

facts.statement: a literary or television premise can be the primary plot or storyline
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster records a primary plot or storyline sense for literary works and television shows.

facts.statement: plural premises can denote land with buildings or a building or part of a building with associated grounds
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster gives both land-with-buildings and building-or-part-of-building formulations.

facts.statement: the verb can offer something as a premise and can base something on certain assumptions
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster records both proposition-as-premise and base-on-assumptions transitive verb senses.

facts.statement: the noun traces through Middle English and Anglo-French to Medieval Latin praemissa and Latin praemittere
facts.source_detail: The word-history section gives the Medieval Latin and Latin source and the sense-specific plural development.

facts.statement: the verb has the inflected forms premised and premising
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster lists premised and premising as the verb's inflected forms.

facts.statement: the noun is pronounced /ˈpremɪs/ and formally denotes a statement or idea forming the basis of a line of argument
facts.source_detail: Oxford lists /ˈpremɪs/ and defines the noun as a statement or idea forming the basis of a reasonable line of argument.

facts.statement: premiss is a less frequent British English variant spelling of the noun
facts.source_detail: Oxford labels premiss as a less frequent British English spelling variant.

facts.statement: the noun comes from Old French premisse and Medieval Latin praemissa (propositio), from Latin praemittere
facts.source_detail: Oxford's word-origin note explicitly gives this historical chain and the prae plus mittere composition.

facts.statement: the noun is an idea or theory on which a statement or action is based
facts.source_detail: Cambridge defines the countable noun in terms of an idea or theory serving as a basis.

facts.statement: the formal transitive verb can base a theory or argument on an idea, thought, or belief
facts.source_detail: Cambridge gives the verb sense and the pattern premise something on something.

facts.statement: the noun has /ˈprem.ɪs/ and the verb is listed with both /prɪˈmaɪz/ and /ˈprem.ɪs/ in UK and US pronunciation
facts.source_detail: Cambridge pronunciation material lists one noun pronunciation and two verb pronunciations for both UK and US.

facts.statement: premise something on something is an attested transitive frame
facts.source_detail: Cambridge explicitly illustrates the frame with an argument premised on assumptions.

facts.statement: in logic a premise is a statement assumed for an argument from which a conclusion is drawn
facts.source_detail: Collins British English explicitly defines the logical premise and its role in drawing a conclusion.

facts.statement: current examples use premise for the central setup of a game, show, or programme
facts.source_detail: Collins examples include the premise of a game, a show's premise, and the basic premise of a time-machine programme.

facts.statement: the transitive verb may take a clause and can mean to state or assume a proposition as a premise
facts.source_detail: Collins marks the verb transitive, notes that it may take a clause as object, and defines proposition-as-premise use.

facts.statement: plural premises can denote the buildings and land occupied by a business or institution
facts.source_detail: Collins COBUILD gives the buildings-and-land sense and on-the-premises examples.

facts.statement: Collins British English lists verb pronunciations /prɪˈmaɪz/ and /ˈprɛmɪs/
facts.source_detail: The British English entry explicitly lists both verb pronunciations.

facts.statement: legal premises can mean matters previously stated, including the preliminary part of a deed
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster Legal records the prior-matters and deed-section senses.

facts.statement: premises can mean a tract of land with component parts such as buildings
facts.source_detail: The legal dictionary directly defines a tract of land with component buildings.

facts.statement: premises can also mean a building or part of a building with appurtenances such as grounds or easements
facts.source_detail: The legal dictionary expressly includes a building or part of a building plus appurtenances.

facts.statement: the plural/property form premises is pronounced approximately /ˈpremɪsɪz/
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster Legal supplies the pronunciation ˈpre-mə-səz for premises, corresponding to the article's /ˈpremɪsɪz/ notation.

facts.statement: the logic noun is recorded in late Middle English from Old French and Medieval Latin praemissa, from Latin praemittere
facts.source_detail: Etymonline traces the late-14th-century logic noun through Old French and Medieval Latin to Latin praemittere.

facts.statement: legal 'matter previously stated' developed through deed descriptions into the property sense by the eighteenth century
facts.source_detail: Etymonline connects early legal-document use to descriptions of houses/buildings and dates the house-or-building-with-grounds sense to 1730.

facts.statement: the verb is recorded from the fifteenth century with the sense of stating or setting forth beforehand
facts.source_detail: Etymonline dates the verb to the mid-15th century and describes the introductory/set-forth sense.
